subject: physiology
title: High-Altitude Pulmonary Oedema, Decompression Sickness, and Dysbarism

steps.tx: A life-threatening complication of rapid ascent to altitudes exceeding twenty-five hundred metres is **high-altitude pulmonary oedema**, or HAPE. Hypoxia causes patchy, non-uniform pulmonary arteriolar vasoconstriction, forcing high pulmonary artery pressures into unconstricted capillary beds, precipitating microvascular stress failure and protein-rich alveolar flooding.
steps.say: High-altitude pulmonary oedema arises when uneven hypoxic vasoconstriction overpressurizes unprotected capillaries, causing leakage.

nodes.label: Severe Alveolar Hypoxia at Altitudes Exceeding 2500 Metres
High Pulmonary Artery Pressure Diverted into Unprotected Capillaries
Capillary Stress Failure and Alveolar Exudate: Severe HAPE

steps.tx: Unlike cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, HAPE is a non-cardiogenic hydrostatic oedema characterized by normal left atrial and pulmonary capillary wedge pressures. Immediate definitive treatment mandates rapid **emergency descent**, administration of high-flow supplemental oxygen, and portable hyperbaric chambers alongside calcium channel blockers like nifedipine.
steps.say: Immediate descent and supplemental oxygen are lifesaving in HAPE, with nifedipine reducing elevated pulmonary vascular pressure.

vis.caption: Severe pulmonary vasoconstriction, vascular stress failure, and secondary right ventricular overload.

steps.tx: Underwater diving exposes the human body to elevated ambient hydrostatic pressures conforming to **Boyle law and Henry law**. For every ten metres of descent in seawater, ambient pressure increases by one atmosphere; Henry law dictates that the amount of ambient gas dissolved in circulating blood increases in direct proportion to ambient pressure.
steps.say: Underwater pressure increases by one atmosphere every ten metres, driving more gas into blood according to Henry law.

rows: Extreme narcosis; high risk of decompression sickness

steps.tx: Because nitrogen is highly lipophilic, breathing compressed air at depths exceeding thirty metres forces immense quantities of dissolved nitrogen into neuronal cell membranes. Known as **nitrogen narcosis**, or rapture of the deep, this produces progressive euphoria, impaired cognitive judgement, and motor incoordination similar to alcohol intoxication.
steps.say: Dissolved nitrogen dissolves into neuronal membranes at depths beyond thirty metres, producing alcohol-like nitrogen narcosis.

left.title: Nitrogen Narcosis
points: Occurs at depths exceeding 30 to 40 metres
Direct anesthetic effect of lipophilic nitrogen gas
Produces euphoria, confusion, and sensory loss
Promptly reverses on ascending to shallower depths

right.title: High-Pressure Neurological Syndrome
points: Occurs at extreme depths (>150 m) on helium-oxygen trimix
Direct mechanical effect of hydrostatic pressure on proteins
Produces tremors, myoclonus, nausea, and EEG changes
Managed by adding small percentages of narcotic nitrogen

steps.tx: If a diver ascends too rapidly toward the surface, ambient pressure drops precipitously, causing supersaturated dissolved nitrogen to come out of physical solution as bubbles, producing **decompression sickness**. Nitrogen bubbles lodge within periarticular tissues causing agonizing joint pain known as the bends, or occlude spinal cord microvessels causing paraplegia.
steps.say: Rapid ascent causes dissolved nitrogen to bubble out of solution, causing agonizing joint pain and neurological deficits.

nodes.label: Deep Dive: High Ambient Pressure Drives Large Nitrogen Load into Tissues
Rapid Ascent Without Staged Decompression Decompresses Gas Abruptly
Supersaturated Nitrogen Gas Forms Insoluble Intravascular Bubbles

steps.tx: Definitive medical management of severe decompression sickness and arterial gas embolism requires immediate administration of hundred percent normobaric oxygen followed by urgent **hyperbaric recompression therapy**. Placing the patient inside a hyperbaric recompression chamber at two point eight atmospheres mechanically shrinks bubble diameter while delivering super-saturated oxygen to ischaemic tissues.
steps.say: Hyperbaric recompression therapy is the definitive treatment for decompression sickness, shrinking nitrogen bubbles and oxygenating tissues.

left.title: Type I Decompression Sickness
points: Mild form restricted to musculoskeletal and cutaneous systems
Periarticular dull throbbing joint pain (the bends)
Cutis marmorata, pruritus, and localized lymphatic swelling

right.title: Type II Decompression Sickness
points: Life-threatening involvement of spinal cord, brain, or lungs
Spinal cord infarction causing paraplegia and bladder dysfunction
Pulmonary microvascular embolization causing tachypnoea (the chokes)
Requires immediate emergency hyperbaric recompression chamber

steps.tx: Breathing oxygen at excessive partial pressures causes **acute oxygen toxicity**, mediated by unrestrained production of reactive oxygen species. Central nervous system toxicity (the Paul Bert effect) triggers grand mal seizures at pressures above two atmospheres, whereas prolonged pulmonary exposure (the Lorrain Smith effect) causes severe tracheobronchitis and atelectasis.
steps.say: Excessive oxygen tension produces reactive oxygen species, triggering seizures in the brain and diffuse damage in the lungs.

rows: Visual tunnels, ear ringing, twitching, grand mal seizures
Substernal burning, dry cough, diffuse alveolar damage
Hyperoxia downregulates VEGF; secondary neovascular blindness

steps.tx: Extreme environmental thermal stress causes severe failure of hypothalamic thermoregulation. When core body temperature rises above forty degrees Celsius accompanied by central nervous system dysfunction and anhidrosis, the patient has **classical heat stroke**. Treatment mandates aggressive, rapid evaporative and conductive whole-body cooling to halt widespread end-organ apoptosis.
steps.say: Heat stroke causes hyperthermia above forty degrees Celsius with delirium, demanding immediate evaporative cooling.

vis.caption: Thermoregulatory failure, evaporative cooling breakdown, and systemic heat-stroke pathophysiology.
